name: Arkansas v. Oklahoma
event: Both petitions challenge the judgment invalidating EPA’s federal discharge permit for Fayetteville’s sewage-treatment plant.
questions: Whether EPA may condition this upstream federal permit on downstream state standards; whether existing downstream degradation categorically bars the discharge; and whether EPA’s compliance interpretation and supported technical findings survive judicial review.
baseline: The four February 26 events are uncoordinated and share a start-of-day baseline including the committed February 25 decisions. None uses another February 26 decision as earlier law.
record: Fayetteville applied in 1985 for a permit; effluent travels through creeks and the Illinois River for about 39 miles to Oklahoma. The permit includes numerical conditions and modification if a study requires tighter limits for Oklahoma compliance. EPA’s Chief Judicial Officer replaced an undue-impact test with a preponderance showing of no actual detectable violation. The ALJ made component-specific findings meeting that direction, sustained by EPA. Arkansas contests an obligatory downstream rule; EPA defends its authority and actual determination; Oklahoma seeks protection of scenic-water standards. The Tenth Circuit imposed an already-degraded-waters prohibition not advanced by a party, without displacing the no-detectable-violation finding. The separate White River discharge is outside review.
entering: Clean Water Act §§301, 303, 401 and 402 (33 U.S.C. §§1311, 1313, 1341, 1342), including §402(a)(2)’s permit-condition authority; 40 C.F.R. §§122.4(d) and 122.44(d); the relevant Oklahoma standards incorporated in the federal permitting process. Milwaukee II, 451 U.S. 304, displaces federal nuisance common law; Ouellette, 479 U.S. 481, restricts affected-state common-law control without eliminating statutory safeguards. Chevron, 467 U.S. 837, and Seminole Rock, 325 U.S. 410, supply the received agency-interpretation framework. Universal Camera, 340 U.S. 474, requires whole-record substantial-evidence review; State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, governs arbitrary-and-capricious review. The administrative preponderance burden differs from appellate substantial-evidence review. Simulated Lechmere (January 27) preserves deference within controlling statutory precedent; simulated NCIR (December 16) accepts a source-supported regulatory construction; Elias-Zacarias (January 22) rejects substituting a merely permissible factual inference for a supported agency finding under its own statute. None conflicts with the permit scheme. Wyoming’s retained original proceeding concerns a different regulatory limitation.
reach: Both dockets concern the same federal permit. EPA’s authority, the categorical bar, incorporated-standard construction and supported application are reached. A universal statutory duty for every state or federal permit, independent source-state tort remedies, new scientific thresholds and later water conditions are not decided.
stoneCheck: Lechmere and the February 25 holdings leave the approved statutory delegation and record-review premises intact. Stone joins the actual permit authority and review holdings, changing neither EPA’s proof burden nor numerical conditions. His join does not turn technical expertise into authority or label all small pollution permissible.
action: The Tenth Circuit is reversed unanimously in both dockets. EPA’s reviewed permit determination is sustained under its existing compliance and modification conditions.

components.title: Federal permit, both dockets
components.remedy: Remove the categorical degradation bar; retain the permit’s existing standards, study and modification conditions.

opinions.author: Stevens
opinions.scope: Federal permit authority, no categorical statutory bar, incorporated standards and administrative review.

assignment: Stone assigns Stevens from the unanimous reversal coalition.

holdings.title: EPA may require downstream standards in this federal permit
holdings.rule: The Clean Water Act authorizes EPA, in issuing this federal permit under §402(a), to require compliance with applicable downstream state water-quality standards through its valid regulations. A downstream State’s limited direct role in permitting does not restrict that federal authority; whether the Act itself commands identical compliance in every permitting setting remains open.
holdings.authority: Stevens’s opinion, joined by all other Justices; unanimous statutory-authority holding.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that EPA acted within Congress’s delegation when it protected Oklahoma’s water standards through the federal permit. Section 402(a)(2) gives the Administrator substantial authority to prescribe permit conditions, and §301(b)(1)(C) identifies attainment of applicable water-quality standards as a statutory objective. Regulation §122.4(d), requiring assurance of affected-state compliance, reasonably carries out that scheme. Milwaukee II identifies the Act’s displacement of federal nuisance law, while Ouellette limits an affected State’s independent common-law and direct permitting role. Neither case bars the federal agency from imposing conditions Congress authorized. Arkansas’s contrary argument confuses limits on a State’s own authority with limits on EPA’s delegated power. Chevron supports this reasonable exercise of that power; expertise alone would not create it. Because the actual federal permit lies within the authorized approach, the Court does not decide whether Congress compels the same formulation in every federal or state permit, or whether an independent source-state remedy applies.
precedents: *Milwaukee v. Illinois*, 451 U.S. 304 — preserved: the statutory water-pollution scheme displaces federal nuisance common law.
*International Paper Co. v. Ouellette*, 479 U.S. 481 — distinguished: affected-state common-law and direct-input limits do not constrain this delegated EPA condition.
*Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc.*, 467 U.S. 837 — applied within Congress’s actual delegation; no overhaul of agency deference.
*Lechmere, Inc. v. NLRB*, simulated January 27, 1992 — preserved: deference operates within controlling statutory precedent, and no contrary construction is displaced here.

holdings.title: Existing degradation is not a categorical statutory prohibition
holdings.rule: The Clean Water Act does not categorically forbid a new discharge merely because its effluent will reach waters already failing a water-quality standard, irrespective of whether it will cause a detectable violation under the applicable permit standards. Courts may not substitute that categorical prohibition for the Act’s actual permitting and pollution-reduction scheme.
holdings.authority: Stevens’s unanimous opinion rejects the independent statutory basis on which the court of appeals invalidated the permit.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that the court of appeals added a prohibition Congress did not enact. The Act contains duties directed toward meeting water-quality standards and provisions for reducing existing pollution, including §303(d)’s framework for allocating reduction burdens. It does not say that every additional source must be barred whenever receiving waters already are degraded. Section 402(h), on which the lower court relied, concerns additional pollutants accepted by a treatment plant violating its own permit; it does not create the broader downstream prohibition. Milwaukee II’s recognition of a comprehensive statutory program is not authority to replace that program with a court’s preferred environmental policy. Existing degradation remains relevant when the governing standards make it so, but it does not eliminate the need to evaluate the proposed discharge under those standards. EPA applied the required no-detectable-violation approach here. The Court neither excuses a detectable violation nor decides later permit conditions on facts outside this record.
precedents: *Milwaukee v. Illinois*, 451 U.S. 304 — its description of a comprehensive program does not authorize an additional judicial categorical ban.

holdings.title: Reasonable construction of the incorporated downstream standards
holdings.rule: For this interstate federal permit, EPA’s valid regulation incorporates the applicable, federally approved downstream standards into federal permitting law, and its reasonable, consistently held construction receives substantial deference. EPA permissibly construed Oklahoma’s no-degradation requirement to prohibit an actual detectable or measurable violation, rather than every infinitesimal theoretical effect.
holdings.authority: Stevens’s unanimous opinion controls the interpretation of the standards as used in this federal permit; it does not decide state law for unrelated purposes.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that the reviewing court must respect EPA’s permissible construction of the standards governing its federal permit. The standards were developed with federal guidance, approved by EPA and incorporated through Regulation §122.4(d); in this interstate permitting setting, they operate as part of federal water-pollution law. Chevron and the received regulatory-deference principle reflected in Seminole Rock support deference to a reasonable, consistently held interpretation within that framework. Requiring a detectable or measurable violation provides a means to determine compliance and does not make every theoretical molecule of additional effluent a downstream veto. NCIR’s source-specific acceptance of a supported regulatory construction is consistent with that approach. The contrary categorical reading lacks support in the statutory or regulatory text. The Court preserves actual standards and their enforcement: it does not announce a general exemption for pollution described as trivial, excuse unreliable science, or confer authority to disregard a demonstrated detectable violation.
precedents: *Chevron U.S.A. Inc. v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc.*, 467 U.S. 837 — applied to the authorized federal permitting construction.
*Bowles v. Seminole Rock & Sand Co.*, 325 U.S. 410 — its received regulatory-interpretation principle remains operative within valid delegated authority.
*INS v. National Center for Immigrants’ Rights, Inc.*, simulated December 16, 1991 — consistent source-specific regulatory construction is applied without importing immigration rules.

holdings.title: Supported findings govern review of this permit
holdings.rule: A reviewing court must accept agency adjudicative findings supported by substantial evidence on the record as a whole and may not replace them merely because competing findings also could be supported. Here EPA’s supported finding that Fayetteville carried the administrative preponderance burden of no actual detectable violation sustains the permit; the court’s contrary policy does not establish arbitrary agency action.
holdings.authority: Stevens’s unanimous opinion controls both the appellate-review rule and its application to the reviewed permit.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that the permit survives review on the record actually decided by EPA. Universal Camera requires substantial evidence supporting the agency’s findings on the whole record, not evidence from which the reviewing court could make different findings. The ALJ addressed nutrient enrichment, appearance, dissolved oxygen and metals under the corrected no-detectable-violation standard and found the city’s preponderance burden satisfied. The identified errors concerning phosphorus in streams and the standards’ edition are harmless here: the findings addressed the more vulnerable lake, and the relevant editions did not materially differ. State Farm requires attention to important aspects of the problem, but the lower court made existing degradation decisive only by adopting its erroneous categorical rule. It could not then label EPA arbitrary for failing to follow that invented rule. The existing study and modification conditions remain safeguards for further information. No new discharge limit, scientific threshold or finding about later water quality is imposed.
precedents: *Universal Camera Corp. v. NLRB*, 340 U.S. 474 — applied: supported agency findings are not displaced by merely permissible alternative findings.
*Motor Vehicle Manufacturers Association v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co.*, 463 U.S. 29 — applied to the actual governing problem, not a court-created categorical policy.

law: Effective February 26, the federal permit scheme authorizes the downstream-compliance approach, rejects the categorical already-degraded-waters bar and sustains the supported no-detectable-violation determination. Before this event those precise statutory and permit applications were unresolved; afterward these rules govern at their stated federal-permit scope. EPA’s administrative preponderance burden, whole-record review, valid conditions and modification mechanism remain distinct and unchanged. General deference, state-law remedies and mandatory duties outside this setting are not revised.
procedure: Supreme Court review ends in both dockets. EPA’s permit determination is sustained with its existing compliance, study and modification conditions. No new limit or order concerning the White River discharge is entered; no future scientific finding or Supreme Court supervision is presumed.
dependencies: Later permit disputes must distinguish statutory authority from a mandatory obligation, and administrative proof from judicial review. The January 22 Wyoming injunction and retained jurisdiction remain separate.
formBasis: unanimous judgment and full opinion; the same non-Stone positions, controlling rules, permit relief and precedent treatment remain. The paired dockets and four holdings are retained at full substantive depth.
sourceMap: 503 U.S. 94–98 verifies the permit, history, burden and appellate theory; pages 101–108 the statutory text and reserved mandatory-duty issue; pages 109–114 the incorporated standards, two harmless errors, detailed findings and review. The full opinion verifies both dockets and December 11 argument.

alternatives: Invalidating downstream conditions confuses the State’s limited independent role with EPA’s federal authority. Accepting that authority does not establish a universal congressional command. A categorical degradation ban conflicts with the enacted program; a remand for technical reconsideration lacks a material record defect after the component findings and harmless errors are examined. The two proof standards serve different actors and are never interchanged.
auditFinal: Both docket judgments and all four operative propositions command nine votes. No scientific finding, new burden or mandatory rule is generated mechanically. The same neutral commitments remain compatible after the Lechmere/NCIR refresh; no material non-Stone revision.
